evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六; lines 122–127
evidence.text: The database reports competing explanations: early 六 and 入 are graphically alike and may once have been one graph, with added strokes later distinguishing the numeral; another proposal treats 六 as a shelter picture and an earlier graph for 廬; a third treats it as a conventional early counting mark. It regards the Shuowen explanation through 易 numerology as unlikely to preserve the graph’s original meaning. It cites oracle-bone numeral uses as cardinal in 合集 32320 (‘燎六羊’) and ordinal in 合集 7775 (‘今六月王入于商’), then gives numeral examples from bronzes and Warring States texts. These citations support numeral use in the cited oracle-bone records, not a chronology among the proposed graphic origins.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六

evidence.source: 字源考釋 - 六, 香港教育城相關字源資源
evidence.text: The page labels a sequence of oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal, and standard forms, and says the first three resemble a front view of a shelter, the original graph for 廬, later borrowed for the number six. The page supplies no argument dating this interpretation or evidence for the pronunciation of the supposed shelter name. Its images were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 六

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction table and system notes; lines 0–34, 108 and 217
evidence.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese version 1.1 (2014), 六 has Mandarin liù, Middle Chinese transcription ljuwk, and Old Chinese *k.ruk, gloss ‘six’; 廬 has Mandarin lú, Middle Chinese transcription ljo, and Old Chinese *[r]a, gloss ‘hut; inn; to lodge’. The authors describe MC as a transcription based on historical sources, not a reconstruction, and say brackets mark uncertainty. These character-word entries do not independently establish that the object depicted by 六 was called 廬; the compared reconstructions do not substantiate the proposed sound-based loan. The local row checked for 六 in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv, row 2140, agrees with the published table.
evidence.kind: primary reconstruction table and system description
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.text: This secondary character entry calls the origin unclear and summarizes a possible 入 differentiation account and a hut pictograph thought to be the earlier form of 廬; it says the numeral meaning is a phonetic loan under either account. It labels oracle script (~1250–1000 BC), early Western Zhou bronze (~1000 BC), Shuowen seal (~100 AD), and Eastern Han clerical exemplars. These labels date displayed script examples, not the origin of the numeral sense. Its historical pronunciation table gives *k.ruk, ljuwk, liù.
evidence.title: 六 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通
evidence.field: 六: dated examples; character form and readings; lines 56–73 and 104–123
evidence.text: The dictionary records Japanese むゆ in a Nihon Shoki example dated 720 (the cited manuscript reading tradition), and in 年中行事秘抄 from the late 12th century. It records ろく for ‘six’ in a late-8th-century Man'yōshū example. These date Japanese lexical attestations, not the Chinese graph’s origin. 字通 endorses a small-shelter interpretation of oracle-bone and bronze forms, says the graph was borrowed for six, and notes that the seal form is not the graph’s initial form; this remains one account among competing proposals.
evidence.kind: historical dictionary with dated Japanese attestations and paleographic account
evidence.title: 六（読み）ロク - コトバンク

evidence.text: The entry presents three competing explanations for 六: it may have once been graphically identical to 入 and later differentiated; it may depict a shelter and be an earlier graph for 廬; or it may be an early conventional counting mark. It considers the Shuowen 易-based explanation unlikely to preserve the graph’s original meaning. It cites oracle-bone examples for cardinal use (合集 32320, “燎六羊”) and ordinal use (合集 7775, “今六月王入于商”). These attest numeral use in the cited records but do not establish which origin theory is correct or the relative chronology of the senses.

gaps: The graphic origin remains unresolved: sources report the 入-related differentiation proposal, a shelter/廬 proposal, and a conventional counting-mark possibility. The inscriptions cited by CUHK support numeral use but do not settle which graphic account is correct.

The shelter-name hypothesis is not phonologically established. The object/name is not independently recovered, and Baxter–Sagart lists distinct reconstructed forms for 六 and 廬. This does not disprove every possible proposal, but does not support a sound-based borrowing from 廬.

CUHK cites oracle-bone records 合集 32320 and 7775 for cardinal and ordinal uses, but the original inscription images and exact excavation/inscription dates were not inspected. The earliest semantic transition and chronology between cardinal and ordinal use remain unestablished.

Later graphic stages and any specific graphic corruption were not established by visual inspection. Online entries label stages or provide inaccessible-to-text glyph images; no specific transformation should be asserted from this run.

The required Unicode Unihan per-character records for 六 (U+516D) and 廬 (U+5EEC) could not be accessed. The local Unihan row liù is not emitted as externally verified evidence; the accessible official Taiwanese record supports modern Mandarin liù for 六 only.

No independent early dated Chinese lexical evidence beyond the cited oracle-bone examples was opened. Japanese dated uses are later language-specific evidence and do not date the Chinese graph’s origin.

The graph’s origin remains unresolved among the 入-differentiation, shelter/廬, and counting-mark proposals. The consulted primary paleographic entry reports these as alternatives; the numeral-use examples do not decide among them.

The proposed shelter-name borrowing is not independently established: the depicted object’s name and pronunciation are unrecovered in the inspected evidence. The proposed loan from 廬 therefore remains unsupported as a sound-based explanation; no pronunciation match is inferred here.

CUHK cites oracle-bone cardinal and ordinal examples, but the original inscription images and exact dates of the individual records were not inspected. Their relative semantic chronology remains open.

The opened official Unihan endpoint for 六 was inaccessible, and the required current kMandarin reading was not verified from that record. The Taiwan CNS11643 record supports liù as modern Mandarin metadata only.
No exact character-specific Xiaoxuetang result or inspectable CC0 notice was retrieved in this run. Commons pages support the proposed image candidates and their stated licensing instead.

The proposed Commons images are modern digital drawings of ancient script forms, not photos of inscribed artifacts. Their labels indicate script traditions; the candidate files do not independently settle the graphic origin.
